data.title: Legitimacy Borrowed From Co-Opted Trusted Voices
data.summary:
Genuine individuals with established audiences — commentators, community figures, in some
cases the organisation's own staff — were induced to carry campaign claims, lending
credibility the operation could not manufacture.
data.description:
Co-option is the hardest element to address because the people carrying the message are
real, usually sincere, and often sympathetic to the audience. They were given material
that appeared credible and passed it on, which is not misconduct.

The campaign benefits twice: the claim arrives from a trusted source, and any response
from the organisation appears to attack a real person with their own following. That
asymmetry is deliberate and should be stated, because the instinctive corporate response
walks directly into it.

Where the co-opted voice is a member of staff, this is an internal matter first. Treating
it as a disciplinary issue rather than as a successful operation against the organisation
usually produces a second, worse story.
data.recommendation:
* Approach co-opted individuals privately with the underlying evidence; most correct the
  record when shown the provenance.
* Do not respond publicly in terms that attack the individual, which is the outcome the
  campaign is designed to produce.
* Where staff are involved, handle it as a successful operation against the organisation
  rather than as misconduct.
data.short_recommendation: Approach co-opted voices privately with the provenance evidence.
